evidence: The sequence matches human LRP4 (MEGF7), an LDLR-family co-receptor that works with MuSK at the neuromuscular junction and in Wnt signalling. I know of no established evidence that it serves as a virus entry receptor, unlike LDLR, VLDLR, LRP8 or LRP1, though this rests on recalled literature rather than a check.

This is human LRP4, identified by its N-terminus and its ~1900-residue LDLR-class/YWTD β-propeller architecture. It acts as the agrin receptor activating MuSK and as a Wnt/sclerostin modulator, and there is no evidence that it binds cholesterol directly.

This sequence matches human LRP4, a single-pass receptor that binds agrin and forms a complex with MuSK. It acts as a molecular bridge that assembles the agrin–LRP4–MuSK signaling complex, which fits adaptor activity; whether GO actually annotates LRP4 with this term was not confirmed.

The sequence is human LRP4, a transmembrane LDL receptor-related protein made of LDL-A repeats, EGF modules and YWTD beta-propellers. It acts as the agrin/Wnt co-receptor at the cell surface, and there is no evidence that it binds nucleosomes.

This looks like human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a soluble NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase family enzyme expected to be cytosolic. It has no signal peptide or transmembrane segment, and I cannot recall whether imaging-based data place it at the Golgi.

This sequence is human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), an SDR-family nucleotide-sugar dehydratase, and its physiological role in humans is poorly defined. Loss-of-function variants cause Catel-Manzke syndrome, and a link to proteoglycan/glycosaminoglycan synthesis has been proposed but, to my knowledge, not firmly established, so direct involvement in GAG biosynthesis is unclear.

This is human TGDS, which UniProt annotates as dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase. It has the conserved short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase features of that enzyme family: the GxxGxxG NAD-binding motif and the catalytic YxxxK motif (YASSK), so the term fits, though human enzymatic activity is inferred rather than directly shown.

This is human TGDS, a predicted dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (SDR family). Its expected activity uses dTDP-glucose, not UDP-glucose, and no specific UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity has been shown for the human protein.

This is human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a cytosolic NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase family enzyme linked to Catel-Manzke syndrome. Nothing indicates it localizes specifically to the photoreceptor inner segment.

This is human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a cytosolic NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase family enzyme involved in nucleotide-sugar metabolism. Nothing in the sequence or its known biology points to a role in cell surface receptor signaling.

This sequence is a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family enzyme with an N-terminal GxxGxxG NAD-binding motif and a YxxxK catalytic motif, consistent with human dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (TGDS). It has no seven-transmembrane GPCR architecture, so it would not act as a G protein-coupled bile acid receptor.

The sequence matches human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA), a glycolytic enzyme with known roles in glycolysis and actin cytoskeleton regulation. I recall no evidence that it positively regulates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, though this rests on recalled literature rather than a checked annotation record.

This sequence is fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (nearly identical to aldolase A, ALDOA), a glycolytic enzyme that cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Neither its catalytic activity nor its known roles involve building glycosaminoglycans.

This sequence is human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA). I recall, though not with certainty, a report that ALDOA binds CpG oligodeoxynucleotides and enhances TLR9-mediated signaling, which would support positive regulation of the TLR9 pathway.

The sequence is human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA), a glycolytic enzyme that cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. It is not known to repair or remove damaged or toxic metabolites.

This sequence is myeloperoxidase (MPO), a neutrophil azurophil-granule peroxidase. During NET formation MPO moves to the nucleus and works with neutrophil elastase to decondense chromatin, which plausibly supports nucleosome disassembly, though I am not certain this specific annotation exists for MPO.

This is myeloperoxidase (MPO), a neutrophil azurophilic granule heme peroxidase. It associates with chromatin during NET formation and helps decondense it, but I could not confirm direct experimental evidence that MPO itself binds nucleosomes.

This sequence is human myeloperoxidase (MPO). During NET formation, MPO uses H2O2 to drive dissociation of the azurosome protein complex, releasing neutrophil elastase, which fits complex-destabilizing activity.

This sequence is human myeloperoxidase (MPO), a heme peroxidase from neutrophil granules that makes hypochlorous acid for host defense. It has no known role in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.
This is human myeloperoxidase (MPO), a heme peroxidase that uses H2O2 to oxidize halides to hypohalous acids. It has no acyl-CoA or acid-thiol ligase activity.

This sequence is human myeloperoxidase, a heme-dependent peroxidase that makes hypochlorous acid in neutrophil granules. Its known roles are catalytic plus some binding (heme, heparin, chromatin), with no evidence that it scaffolds or bridges other macromolecules as an adaptor.

This is human LAMP2, isoform A (it has the GLKHHHAGYEQF C-terminal tail), the receptor for chaperone-mediated autophagy. Published work reports that LAMP2A-mediated chaperone-mediated autophagy degrades GPX4, which promotes ferroptosis, consistent with positive regulation of ferroptosis.

This is LAMP2 (lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 2, the LAMP2A isoform with the C-terminal GYEQF motif). It is a lysosomal membrane protein involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy, and I know of no role for it in adenylate cyclase-activating GPCR signaling.

This sequence is LAMP2 (lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 2), a heavily glycosylated lysosomal membrane protein involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy and lysosome function. There is no evidence it acts in the IFT-A/dynein-2 retrograde intraflagellar transport machinery.

This is LAMP2 (lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 2, isoform A, with the C-terminal GYEQF tail), a lysosomal membrane protein that acts as the receptor in chaperone-mediated autophagy. It is not a mitochondrial carrier, and mitochondrial CoA import is done by SLC25 family transporters such as SLC25A42.
The sequence matches human SLC25A16 (Graves disease carrier protein). It is the ortholog of yeast Leu5 and transports coenzyme A into mitochondria across the inner membrane.

The sequence has the repeated mitochondrial carrier (SLC25 family) signature motifs with transmembrane solute-transport architecture. It has no domains associated with DNA damage recognition or repair, so involvement in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair is not expected.

This is a mitochondrial carrier (SLC25 family) transporter of the inner mitochondrial membrane, with the characteristic repeated carrier-domain motifs. Nothing in it suggests a role in GPCR or adenylate-cyclase-activating signaling.

The sequence looks like SLC25A16 (Graves disease carrier protein), a mitochondrial coenzyme A/CoA-precursor carrier of about 332 residues. Nothing I know of links it to positive regulation of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, so the term is unlikely to apply.

This sequence is human spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK): tandem SH2 domains, ITAM-binding linker, and a C-terminal tyrosine kinase domain. SYK is reported to be required for TLR9-driven responses in B cells, supporting positive regulation of TLR9 signaling, though I could not confirm a specific annotation for this term and SYK may instead dampen TLR9 output in plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

This is human spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK): tandem SH2 domains followed by a C-terminal tyrosine kinase domain. Its established roles are in immunoreceptor (BCR/FcR) signaling, and I know of no evidence placing it in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair, so this is a best-judgment call rather than a confirmed absence.
This sequence is ZAP-70, a T-cell receptor-associated tyrosine kinase with tandem SH2 domains and a C-terminal kinase domain. It acts in TCR signaling and has no known role in non-stop mRNA decay.

This sequence is ZAP-70, a tyrosine kinase with tandem SH2 domains and a C-terminal kinase domain that signals downstream of the T-cell receptor. It has no enzymatic role in repairing or removing damaged or toxic metabolites.

This sequence is beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), a GPCR desensitization, internalization and scaffolding adaptor. Its documented links to metabolism are mostly indirect or systemic (for example, insulin signaling and beta-cell studies, which are better established for ARRB2), and I recall no specific evidence that ARRB1 itself maintains intracellular glucose homeostasis.

This sequence is beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1). It binds activated, phosphorylated GPCRs to desensitize and internalize them, and it scaffolds receptor-dependent signaling such as MAPK/ERK activation, so it takes part in G protein-coupled receptor signaling, a form of cell surface receptor signaling.

This sequence is human beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1). Beta-arrestins are recruited to primary cilia and mediate the retrieval and removal of ciliary GPCRs such as GPR161 and SSTR3, which supports this annotation, though the direct evidence is stronger for beta-arrestin-2 than for beta-arrestin-1.

This sequence is human beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1). Beta-arrestins mediate the activity-dependent removal of ciliary GPCRs such as GPR161 and SSTR3 from the ciliary membrane, which fits negative regulation of protein localization to the ciliary membrane, though much of that evidence comes from beta-arrestin-2 or both arrestins together.

This is human beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), an adaptor that desensitizes and internalizes G-protein-coupled receptors and scaffolds signaling. It has no known catalytic or regulatory role in making glycosaminoglycan chains, so the term does not fit.

This sequence matches human beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), a GPCR desensitization and signaling scaffold with no catalytic role in malate metabolism. Any 'malate metabolic process' annotation could only be indirect, such as one inferred from an orthologue or a phenotype, and I cannot confirm whether one exists.

This sequence is beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), a GPCR desensitization and scaffolding adaptor. It has a reported role in a stress-induced DNA-damage pathway via p53 regulation, but no known direct role in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

The sequence matches human GSK3B (glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta), a multifunctional Ser/Thr kinase. Links between GSK3 and lipid regulators such as SREBP turnover or ABCA1 have been reported, but I can't confirm a direct role for GSK3B in regulating cholesterol transport or efflux.

The sequence matches human glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B), a kinase involved in cardiac development and hypertrophy signaling. I cannot confirm that GSK3B itself is specifically linked to regulating heart rate.

This sequence is human glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B), a Ser/Thr kinase acting in Wnt, insulin and other signaling pathways. I know of no established direct role for it in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair, though GSK3B has very broad annotations and I cannot fully rule out a reported link.

This is human GSK3B, a multifunctional serine/threonine kinase involved in Wnt, insulin and microtubule regulation. It is not a core IFT-A or dynein-2 component, and I know of no specific evidence that it drives retrograde intraciliary transport, though I am not fully certain whether it carries this annotation.

The sequence matches human STK19 (the reannotated 254-aa form made of winged-helix domains), which 2024 studies identified as a transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair factor. In those studies it bound stalled RNA polymerase II together with CSA/UVSSA, so direct binding to the RNA polymerase II complex is supported.

The 254-residue sequence with winged-helix-like motifs is consistent with human STK19 (corrected isoform), though the identification is inferred from the sequence rather than confirmed. Recent studies show STK19 binds the stalled-RNA polymerase II/CSA/UVSSA complex and helps recruit TFIIH, making it a transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair factor.

This looks like human STK19, a winged-helix DNA-binding protein that joins the transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair complex on stalled RNA polymerase II (with CSA, UVSSA and ELOF1). It is not established as a subunit of a transcription elongation factor complex, though this identification is from sequence recall and not certain.

This sequence appears to be human STK19, a winged-helix protein that 2024 studies place in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair. In that pathway it bridges stalled RNA Pol II and associated factors to the TFIIH complex and helps position it, consistent with TFIIH holo complex binding; the identification and annotation are inferred from memory of that work, not verified.

This short human protein has no AMP-binding/adenylate-forming domain or acyl-CoA synthetase motifs. It looks like a small winged-helix nucleic acid-binding protein (STK19-like), so acid-thiol (CoA) ligase activity is not expected.

This sequence looks like STK19, a small winged-helix nucleic-acid-binding protein, not a Rossmann-fold SDR-family nucleotide-sugar dehydratase; it lacks the GxxGxxG NAD-binding motif and catalytic residues. Humans' only related enzyme (TGDS) is a separate protein, so UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity is not expected.

This appears to be STK19, a nuclear winged-helix protein involved in transcription-coupled DNA repair, not a kinase. Neither its sequence features nor its known biology suggest localization to the ciliary tip.

This is the mitochondrial NAD-isocitrate dehydrogenase gamma subunit (IDH3G). It is annotated to the mitochondrion and mitochondrial matrix as part of the IDH3 complex. I don't recall a specific photoreceptor inner segment annotation for it, though this is uncertain.

This sequence matches human IDH3G, the gamma subunit of mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase. It has an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence and acts in the TCA cycle within the mitochondrial matrix, with no expected association with chromatin.

This sequence is IDH3 gamma, the mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase subunit. It has a mitochondrial targeting presequence and works in the TCA cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, with no transmembrane segments or known localization to the endolysosome membrane.

This sequence matches IDH3G, the gamma subunit of mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial-matrix enzyme of the TCA cycle. I cannot recall any annotation placing it at the ciliary tip, though large-scale imaging atlases might have reported one, so confidence is moderate.

This is human SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase. It carries the CoA-binding domain and the catalytic phosphohistidine (GEIGG motif). With the beta subunit SUCLG2, it forms the GTP-specific enzyme that has succinate-CoA ligase (GDP-forming) activity.

This is the mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase alpha subunit (SUCLG1). Its TCA-cycle role is the reversible conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate, not acting on malate. I recall no evidence specifically tying it to malate metabolism, though I can't fully rule out such an annotation.

This is human SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase. It has the CoA-binding domain and the conserved phosphohistidine motif (GEIGG), and catalyzes succinate-CoA ligase activity (GDP/ADP-forming), which is a child of acid-thiol ligase activity.

This is human SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase. Besides its main succinate-CoA ligase activity, this enzyme has a reported promiscuous side activity that converts (S)-malate and CoA to malyl-CoA, which I recall being annotated for this protein, though I have not verified the annotation.

This sequence is SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase, a core TCA-cycle enzyme. Its side activities (e.g., forming malyl-CoA or itaconyl-CoA) create problematic metabolites rather than repair them; repair is done by other enzymes such as CLYBL.

This sequence is SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase (CoA-binding domain plus the ligase domain). Its role is catalytic, forming heterodimers with SUCLA2 or SUCLG2, and nothing points to it acting as a scaffold or adaptor that brings other macromolecules together.

This is SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase, a TCA-cycle matrix enzyme that binds CoA and nucleotides. I know of no established evidence that it binds nucleosomes, though a stray annotation from large-scale proteomic screens cannot be fully ruled out.

This is the mitochondrial succinyl-CoA synthetase alpha subunit (SUCLG1), a CoA-binding TCA-cycle enzyme. It has no known phosphoinositide-binding domain, and I know of no evidence that it specifically binds PI(3,5)P2, though a weak hit from a large-scale lipid-binding screen cannot be fully ruled out.

This sequence is human VLDLR (very low-density lipoprotein receptor), identified by its N-terminus and its eight LDL-receptor class A ligand-binding repeats. VLDLR is a recognized entry receptor for minor-group human rhinoviruses and for alphaviruses such as Semliki Forest virus and eastern equine encephalitis virus.

The sequence is a single-pass membrane receptor of the LDL receptor family (VLDLR-like): it has an N-terminal signal peptide, eight LDLR class A cysteine-rich repeats, EGF-like domains, YWTD beta-propeller repeats, a transmembrane helix and an NPxY cytoplasmic motif. It has none of the CoA-binding or ATP-grasp features of a GDP-forming succinyl-CoA synthetase subunit.

This is the human very-low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR), an LDLR-family transmembrane receptor that binds ligands such as Reelin and ApoE and engages Dab1 through its NPxY motif. Its functions are receptor and ligand-binding activities rather than bridging two macromolecules as an adaptor, though annotation of the adaptor term is not checked here.

This is a human LDL receptor family protein (it looks like LRP8/ApoER2), with LDLR class A repeats, EGF-like domains, YWTD beta-propeller repeats, a transmembrane segment and an NPxY motif. It is a membrane lipoprotein/Reelin receptor with no nucleotide-sugar dehydratase domain, and UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity is not known in humans.

The RING, B-box, coiled-coil and PHD domains with a C-terminal bromodomain-like region suggest this is a TIF1-family protein, most likely TRIM66 (TIF1-delta), though the identification is uncertain. TIF1 proteins are transcriptional corepressors that bind chromatin, and TIF1-delta is reported to associate with HP1 at heterochromatin.

The sequence matches human TRIM28 (KAP1), an 835-aa transcriptional corepressor and SUMO/ubiquitin E3 ligase best known for repressing KRAB zinc-finger targets and IRF7. I cannot recall solid evidence that it specifically suppresses canonical NF-kappaB signaling, so this annotation is plausible but unconfirmed.

The sequence looks like a TIF1-family (TRIM24/28/33/66-like) nuclear transcriptional co-regulator, with RING, B-box, PHD and bromodomain features, most consistent with TRIM66. It is chromatin-associated, and nothing links it to localization in the photoreceptor inner segment.

This is TRIM28 (KAP1/TIF1-beta), a nuclear transcriptional corepressor with RING, B-box, PHD and bromodomain regions. To my knowledge it is localized to the nucleus and chromatin, and I don't recall any Golgi annotation.

The sequence is human TRIM28 (KAP1), with its RING, B-box, coiled-coil, PHD and bromodomain architecture. As I recall, though I can't pin down the specific study, TRIM28 restricts the ciliary-membrane localization of a target protein, likely through ubiquitin/SUMO modification. That would fit negative regulation of protein localization to the ciliary membrane, but confidence is moderate.

This looks like human SKIV2L (SKI2W), the DExH-box RNA helicase of the cytoplasmic SKI complex. That complex works with the exosome on ribosome-associated mRNA decay, including degradation of non-stop mRNAs, as Ski2 does in yeast. The identification rests on sequence features and family knowledge rather than a direct database lookup.

This looks like human SKIV2L (SKI2W), a DEVH-box RNA helicase of the cytoplasmic SKI complex that works with the RNA exosome in 3'-to-5' mRNA decay. I know of no established role for it in regulating cholesterol transport, though I cannot rule out an annotation from a large-scale study.

This sequence is human SKIV2L (SKI2W), the RNA helicase of the cytoplasmic SKI–exosome complex. It is reported to limit RIG-I-like receptor-driven innate immune activation (Eckard et al. 2014), which would include downstream NF-kappaB signaling; I am less sure it is annotated to this exact term than to interferon regulation.

This sequence appears to be human SKIV2L (SKI2W), a cytoplasmic RNA helicase in the SKI complex that works with the exosome in 3'-to-5' mRNA decay. I know of no evidence that it positively regulates Smoothened/Hedgehog signaling; that link belongs to the unrelated SKI proto-oncoprotein.

This appears to be spastizin (ZFYVE26/SPG15), a large FYVE-domain protein whose known interactions are with other partners such as SPG11 and the AP-5 complex. I know of no evidence that it binds itself.

This appears to be spastizin (ZFYVE26), whose FYVE zinc-finger domain binds phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate. It works in autophagy, endolysosomal function and cytokinesis, and there is no recognized evidence that it binds cholesterol directly.

This sequence matches spastizin (ZFYVE26), a large FYVE zinc-finger scaffold protein involved in autophagy, endosomal trafficking and cytokinesis. It has no acyl-CoA synthetase or other acid-thiol ligase domain, and no such catalytic activity is reported for it.

This is human ZFYVE26 (spastizin), a large FYVE zinc-finger protein involved in autophagy and cytokinesis. It has no NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase (SDR) domain, and UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity is not known in humans.

This appears to be a MAS-related G-protein coupled receptor (likely MRGPRE), an orphan GPCR mainly studied in sensory neurons. I know of no well-established evidence that it directly takes part in intracellular glucose homeostasis, though a recently reported metabolic role cannot be ruled out.

This looks like a MAS-related G-protein coupled receptor (likely MRGPRE): it has seven hydrophobic transmembrane segments typical of rhodopsin-like GPCRs. Such receptors sit in the cell-surface plasma membrane.

This looks like human MRGPRE, a Mas-related seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor, identified from sequence features (it is an orphan receptor with no characterized ligand). As a GPCR it falls under G protein-coupled receptor signaling (GO:0007186), which is a child of cell surface receptor signaling pathway.

This looks like an orphan Mas-related GPCR (likely MRGPRE). The Mas-related receptors that have been characterized couple mainly to Gq/Gi, and I know of no evidence that this protein signals by activating adenylate cyclase through Gs.

The sequence looks like an orphan MAS-related G-protein-coupled receptor, most likely MRGPRE, though that identification is not certain. Nothing I know of links that receptor to glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, unlike receptors such as FFAR1 or GPR119.

This sequence looks like an orphan Mas-related GPCR, most likely MRGPRE, though that identification is from memory and not certain. It is not one of the known bile acid–activated GPCRs (GPBAR1/TGR5 or MRGPRX4), and no bile acid ligand has been established for it.

This sequence appears to be MRGPRE, an orphan Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor with no known bile acid ligand. Bile acid-triggered adenylate cyclase signaling is characteristic of GPBAR1 (TGR5), and this protein is not that receptor.

The sequence looks like a Mas-related (MRGPR-family) G-protein-coupled receptor, inferred from sequence features rather than a confirmed match. Nothing known about it suggests localization to the photoreceptor inner segment.

The sequence has seven hydrophobic transmembrane segments and motifs typical of a MAS-related (MRGPR-like) class A G protein-coupled receptor. A receptor of this kind signals as a receptor and would not be expected to act as a protein–macromolecule adaptor or scaffold, though this is inferred from sequence features rather than direct evidence.

The sequence looks like a Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor (probably MRGPRE), an orphan GPCR thought to act in sensory signalling. I know of no evidence that it regulates cholesterol transport, though I cannot rule out an obscure annotation.

This sequence is human STING1 (TMEM173), an ER/Golgi transmembrane adaptor whose trafficking and signalling are regulated by membrane cholesterol. Its transmembrane domain is reported to carry cholesterol-recognition (CRAC-like) motifs that bind cholesterol, though I am not fully certain this annotation is experimentally established.

This sequence is human STING1 (TMEM173). After activation it traffics from the ER through the Golgi to endolysosomes, where it is degraded by ESCRT-dependent microautophagy, so it is plausibly located in the endolysosome membrane. I am recalling this from the literature and am not certain this exact GO term is assigned to it.

This sequence is human STING1 (TMEM173), an ER-to-Golgi trafficking adaptor in the cGAS–STING pathway. As I recall, lipid-binding assays report STING binding to several phosphoinositides including PI(3,5)P2, but I could not verify that specific annotation, so confidence is moderate.

This sequence is human STING1 (TMEM173), a multi-pass membrane protein of the ER, Golgi and perinuclear membranes that signals in innate immunity. It is not known as a chromatin component, though one nuclear-envelope report links it to chromatin compaction.

This sequence is human STING1 (TMEM173), an ER-membrane adaptor that binds cyclic dinucleotides and signals to TBK1/IRF3 in innate immunity. It has no acyl-CoA synthetase or other acid-thiol ligase domain or catalytic activity.

This is human STING (TMEM173), an ER-resident adaptor in cytosolic DNA/cyclic-dinucleotide innate immune signaling, not a seven-transmembrane GPCR. It has no reported G protein-coupled bile acid receptor activity (that function belongs to GPBAR1/TGR5).

This looks like phospholipase D family member 5 (PLD5), a single-pass membrane protein of the PLD3/PLD4 type II membrane subfamily, which is linked to the ER and endolysosomal system. It has no N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence, and I know of no evidence placing it in mitochondria.

This looks like a member of the PLD3/4/5 phospholipase D-like family (likely PLD5), which are type II transmembrane glycoproteins found in the endolysosomal and ER membranes. Nothing in the sequence or known biology suggests a chromatin association.

This looks like PLD5, a catalytically inactive member of the phospholipase D family. It is a poorly characterized single-pass type II membrane protein, and I know of no evidence placing it specifically in the Golgi apparatus; relatives such as PLD3 are reported mainly in the ER and endolysosomes.

This looks like human PLD5, a catalytically inactive member of the PLD3/4/5 phospholipase D family (536 aa, type II membrane protein with degenerate HKD motifs). As far as I know, no annotation or experimental evidence places it at the ciliary tip.

This looks like human STK36 (Fused homolog), a Hedgehog-pathway and ciliary central-pair kinase. It binds partners such as KIF27, SPAG16 and ULK4, which hints at a scaffolding role, but I can't confirm that it is documented as a protein-macromolecule adaptor itself rather than as a kinase.

This sequence matches human ULK4, a pseudokinase. ULK4 has been reported (Zhou et al., Jiang lab) to promote Sonic hedgehog signaling by working with Stk36/Fused to support Gli2 phosphorylation and activation in primary cilia, which fits positive regulation of the smoothened pathway.

This is human STK36 (Fused homolog), a kinase in Hedgehog signalling. Work on Stk36 and Ulk4 (Zhou, Han & Jiang, eLife 2023, recalled from memory) reports that Stk36 accumulates at the primary cilium tip after Shh stimulation, so a ciliary-tip annotation is likely.

This looks like ULK4, a large pseudokinase with an N-terminal kinase-like domain and a C-terminal HEAT/ARM-repeat region. I don't recall a Golgi localization for it from experimental or curated sources, and the sequence has no clear Golgi-targeting features, so I can neither confirm nor rule out the annotation.

This looks like human ULK4, a large pseudokinase of the Unc-51-like kinase family. Its known roles are in neural development, cilia and neuronal migration, and I know of no evidence linking it to glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

This appears to be human ULK4, an unc-51-like pseudokinase with an N-terminal kinase-like domain and a long C-terminal ARM/HEAT-like region. As far as I know, no binding to the TFIIH holo complex has been reported or annotated for it.

This sequence appears to be ERLEC1 (XTP3-B), an ER lectin with two MRH domains. ERLEC1 binds SEL1L and is a component of the HRD1 (SYVN1) ERAD E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, so it belongs to the Hrd1p ubiquitin ligase complex.

This looks like human ERLEC1 (XTP3-B), a two-MRH-domain ER lectin related to yeast Yos9, which is part of the luminal surveillance complex. ERLEC1 associates with SEL1L-HRD1 to recognize misfolded glycoproteins for ERAD, so membership in this complex is likely, though I am inferring it rather than recalling a specific annotation.

This sequence has two MRH (mannose-6-phosphate receptor homology) lectin domains and a signal peptide, consistent with ERLEC1/XTP3-B. That is an ER-lumenal lectin involved in ER-associated degradation (ERAD), not a chromatin-associated protein.

This looks like ERLEC1 (XTP3-B), a lectin with two MRH domains that works in ER-associated degradation and lives in the ER lumen. I know of no strong evidence placing it in the Golgi, though stray annotations can't be fully ruled out.

The sequence matches ERLEC1 (XTP3-B), an ER-lumen lectin with MRH domains that acts in ER-associated degradation of misfolded glycoproteins. It has no known role in a nuclear transcription elongation factor complex.

This sequence is human MyD88, identifiable by its N-terminal death domain and C-terminal TIR domain. MyD88 is the essential adaptor that couples TLR9 to IRAK4/IRAK1/TRAF6 downstream signaling, and this is experimentally established in human cells.

This is human MyD88, the TLR/IL-1R adaptor with an N-terminal death domain and a C-terminal TIR domain. Studies in mice suggest MyD88 signaling in hepatocytes and intestinal cells influences glucose metabolism, so annotation to intracellular glucose homeostasis is plausible, but I could not confirm this specific annotation from memory.
This is human MyD88, a TIR/death-domain adaptor that signals downstream of Toll-like and IL-1 receptors. It plays no known role in DNA repair or transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

This sequence is human MyD88, a TIR/death-domain adaptor best known for TLR/IL-1R signaling. It also has a recorded annotation for positively regulating Hedgehog/Smoothened pathway activity, though I am recalling that annotation from memory and only moderately sure of it.

The sequence matches POPDC2 (Popeye domain-containing protein 2), a cAMP-binding membrane protein of cardiac muscle and the conduction system. Popdc2 loss in mice causes stress-induced sinus node dysfunction and bradycardia, consistent with a role in heart rate regulation.

This looks like POPDC2 (Popeye domain-containing protein 2), a membrane protein with a cAMP-binding Popeye domain involved in cardiac and skeletal muscle signaling. It has no chromatin-remodeling or histone-chaperone features that would point to a role in nucleosome disassembly.

This looks like a Popeye domain-containing protein (likely POPDC2), a cAMP-binding membrane protein known mainly for roles in heart and skeletal muscle. I know of no evidence that it positively regulates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

This sequence looks like a Popeye domain-containing protein (likely POPDC2, 364 aa), a membrane protein with a cAMP-binding domain that acts in cardiac and skeletal muscle signaling. It is not a mitochondrial carrier (SLC25) and has no known role in moving coenzyme A across mitochondrial membranes.

This appears to be kallikrein-related peptidase 11 (KLK11, the longer isoform), a trypsin-like serine protease that is secreted. Any passage through the Golgi would be transient secretory trafficking, and I recall no specific Golgi-resident localization for it, though that recollection is not certain.

This sequence is kallikrein-11 (KLK11), a trypsin-like serine protease with a signal peptide that is secreted into the extracellular space. The arginine-rich N-terminal extension of this isoform is suggestive but does not establish mitochondrial localization, and I know of no mitochondrial annotation for KLK11.

The sequence looks like a trypsin-like serine protease of the kallikrein type, with an N-terminal signal sequence and catalytic domain. It lacks a C-terminal transmembrane or GPI-anchor signal, so it is most likely secreted rather than plasma membrane–associated, though the exact protein identity is not certain.

This is a secreted kallikrein-like trypsin-family serine protease, with a signal peptide, His-Asp-Ser catalytic triad and GDSGGP motif. Nothing suggests it belongs to an ER luminal quality-control/ERAD surveillance complex.
